chapters.title: Chapter 3: Hedging a Mutual Fund or Diversified Portfolio with Nifty Options

lessons.title: Sizing the Hedge: How Many Nifty Lots Protect Your Portfolio

children.text: You now know which part of your portfolio a Nifty hedge can protect and how much Nifty exposure it really carries. The last practical question is the one your broker's order screen will ask: how many lots? Get it wrong on the low side and a crash still hurts badly. Get it wrong on the high side and you are quietly betting on a fall, exactly the over-hedging trap from Chapter 1. And because options only come in whole lots worth over ₹16 lakh each, the right answer is rarely a neat whole number. This lesson gives you the formula, the rounding rules, and a clear view of what each choice does to your portfolio.

body.text: Size the hedge to your beta-weighted exposure, not your portfolio's market value, then round to whole lots with your eyes open. Rounding down leaves some risk unprotected. Rounding up adds a bet on a fall. Neither is wrong, as long as you know which one you chose and why.

children.text: The Sizing Formula

body.latex: \text{Lots needed} = \frac{\text{Beta-weighted exposure} \times \text{Target hedge ratio}}{\text{Nifty level} \times \text{Lot size}}
body.caption: Beta-weighted exposure = Σ (value of each holding × its beta). Target hedge ratio = the share you want protected, usually 100% or less.

markDefs.definition: The rupee value of the index exposure one option lot represents: lot size × index level.

children.text: The bottom line of the formula is the
notional value per lot

. With the Nifty at 25,000 and a lot size of 65, one lot represents ₹16,25,000 of Nifty. That number moves every day with the index, which is why a hedge that was correctly sized three months ago may not be today.

body.label: Notional value of one Nifty lot
body.context: At Nifty 22,000 the same lot covers only ₹14,30,000. At 28,000 it covers ₹18,20,000. Always recalculate with today's index level and the current lot size.

children.text: Rohan's Hedge: 1.35 Lots That Do Not Exist
Rohan's ₹25 lakh portfolio has a beta-weighted exposure of ₹21,87,500. He wants a full hedge, so his target hedge ratio is 100%.

body.caption: He can buy 1 lot (74% of his beta-weighted exposure) or 2 lots (149%), but not 1.35.

children.text: Here is what each choice does at expiry, using the three-month 24,000 put at ₹250, and assuming his portfolio moves exactly in line with its beta.

body.caption: Rohan's portfolio at expiry: beta-weighted exposure ₹21,87,500, 24,000 puts at ₹250 (illustrative)

body.title: Rohan's portfolio at expiry: no hedge, 1 lot and 2 lots

children.text: Read the two-lot line carefully. Below the 24,000 strike, it rises as the Nifty falls, and it turns positive below about 21,200. At 20,000, Rohan's portfolio is showing a ₹50,000 profit in a 20% crash. That sounds wonderful until you remember what it means: the extra 0.65 lots are a bet on the market falling. The one-lot line never turns upward. It slows the fall to roughly a quarter of the unhedged slope below the strike, but it never flattens completely.

body.text: There is one legitimate case for rounding up: basis risk. In Lesson 2, a 15% Nifty fall cost Rohan about 16.6% more than beta predicted, because his mid and flexi cap funds fell harder. Apply a similar gap to a 20% fall and his real loss is closer to ₹5,10,000. Then one lot leaves him down ₹2,66,250, while two lots leave him down just ₹22,500. The second lot is not a free bet in a crash like that. It is buffer against basis risk. The price is heavier over-hedging when the market behaves normally, and double the premium.

children.text: Rules for Rounding

columns.label: Round down (under-hedge)
points: Your portfolio is mostly index and large cap funds, with R-squared above 0.9
Your goal has some flexibility, or the tolerable drawdown is not tight
Protection is expensive right now, with India VIX elevated
The exact lot count is only slightly above a whole number, such as 2.2
You would be uncomfortable profiting from a crash

columns.label: Round up (over-hedge)
points: Your portfolio leans towards mid and small caps, with meaningful basis risk
A hard goal is due soon and a shortfall is not acceptable
Protection is cheap, with India VIX low
The exact lot count is close to the next whole number, such as 2.8
You accept that the extra portion is effectively a bet on a fall

children.text: There are also two ways to get closer to the exact number without buying fractional lots:
Shrink the exposure, not the hedge.

If Rohan moved about ₹5 lakh from his mid cap and flexi cap funds into debt, his beta-weighted exposure would fall close to one lot's ₹16.25 lakh. One lot would then be a near-exact full hedge, with less basis risk as a bonus.
Use a closer strike on the lower lot count.

One lot of a 24,500 put, instead of 24,000, starts protecting sooner and partly compensates for the missing 0.35 lots in moderate falls. It does not change the slope below the strike, so it helps less in a deep crash.

body.title: Which way to round?
body.question: Leela, 61, retired, has a ₹48 lakh portfolio of Nifty 50 index funds (beta 1.0, R-squared 0.99). She plans to withdraw ₹35 lakh in four months to buy a flat for her daughter, and India VIX is at 11. Her exact lot count works out to 2.95. What is the most sensible choice?
options: Buy 2 lots, because rounding down is always safer
Buy 3 lots, a 101.6% hedge on a closely tracking portfolio with cheap protection and a hard goal
Skip the hedge, because index funds do not need protection
body.explanation: 2.95 is almost exactly 3, so 3 lots gives a hedge ratio of about 101.6% with negligible over-hedging. Her portfolio tracks the Nifty very closely, her goal is hard and near, and low VIX makes protection cheap. Two lots would leave a third of her exposure unprotected. Four would be a clear bet on a fall.

children.text: How Portfolio Size Changes the Picture

body.caption: Exact and achievable hedges at different portfolio sizes, Nifty at 25,000, lot size 65 (₹16,25,000 per lot)

children.text: The pattern is clear. The bigger the portfolio, the finer the steps, and the easier it is to land near your target. Below roughly one lot of beta-weighted exposure, there is no sensible Nifty options hedge at all: one lot is already a large over-hedge. Each extra lot is a step of ₹16.25 lakh, so at ₹1 crore each lot shifts the hedge ratio by about 15 percentage points, while at ₹25 lakh a single lot shifts it by about 74.

body.title: Count the lots
body.prompt: Arvind's portfolio is worth ₹48 lakh with a portfolio beta of 1.1 against the Nifty 50. The Nifty is at 25,000 and the lot size is 65. For a 100% hedge, how many lots does the formula give? (Two decimal places.)
body.explanation: Beta-weighted exposure = ₹48,00,000 × 1.1 = ₹52,80,000. Notional per lot = 25,000 × 65 = ₹16,25,000. Lots = 52,80,000 ÷ 16,25,000 = 3.25. He can buy 3 lots (about 92% hedged) or 4 lots (about 123% hedged).

body.title: The bottom of the formula
body.textWithBlank: The notional value of one Nifty option lot equals the lot size multiplied by the Nifty ___.
body.explanation: With a lot size of 65 and the Nifty at 25,000, one lot represents ₹16,25,000 of index exposure. If the Nifty rises, each lot covers more rupees of exposure, and you may need fewer lots.

children.text: A Correct Size Today Drifts Tomorrow
Four things quietly change the right number of lots while your hedge sits in place. Recalculate whenever any of them has moved meaningfully, and always at each roll.

body.caption: What makes a hedge size drift
headers: Effect on the lots you need

cells: Portfolio value and notional per lot both move, so the ratio shifts, especially for portfolios with beta far from 1
After a 10% move in the Nifty
Exposure grows every month. A ₹50,000 monthly SIP adds ₹6 lakh a year before returns
Exposure falls, and a previously correct hedge becomes an over-hedge
Fund managers shift holdings between large, mid and small caps
Once a year, or after a change in fund manager or strategy

body.title: Too small for a lot
body.scenario: Swati, 33, a UX designer in Bengaluru, has ₹9 lakh in a Nifty 50 index fund and a ₹25,000 monthly SIP. She has just finished this chapter and is worried about a correction in the next three months. With the Nifty at 25,000, she is considering buying one lot of a three-month 24,000 put at ₹250.
body.prompt: What would one lot mean for Swati's portfolio, and what would you suggest instead?
body.modelAnswer:
1. One lot covers ₹16,25,000 of Nifty against her ₹9 lakh exposure, a hedge ratio of about 181%. The extra ₹7.25 lakh of cover is a pure bet that the market will fall.
2. The premium is ₹16,250, about 1.8% of her portfolio for one quarter. Rolled all year, that is roughly 7% of her portfolio, far more than it costs someone with a correctly sized hedge.
3. In a sharp fall she would profit, but in a flat or rising market she loses the full premium on cover she mostly did not need.
4. More importantly, she has a long horizon, a steady SIP and no near-term goal from Lesson 2 of Chapter 1. A correction lets her SIP buy more units cheaply. Her real risk is stopping the SIP in a panic, not the fall itself.
5. Sensible alternatives: no hedge at all, with a written commitment to keep the SIP running; or, if she has a specific goal coming up, moving that amount to a debt fund.
The lesson: below about one lot of beta-weighted exposure, Nifty options cannot hedge a portfolio. They can only speculate on it.

body.title: Show me the math: Rohan's 20% fall with and without basis risk

children.text: The beta-predicted loss is ₹21,87,500 × 20% = ₹4,37,500. The basis gap uses Lesson 2's ratio: ₹3,82,500 actual ÷ ₹3,28,125 predicted ≈ 1.166, so ₹4,37,500 × 1.166 ≈ ₹5,10,000. This is one plausible stress outcome, not a forecast. In a milder fall, or one led by large caps, the gap could be smaller or even reverse.

body.title: Size your own hedge
steps: Take the beta-weighted exposure you calculated in Lesson 2, and remove any part you do not intend to protect.
Look up today's Nifty level and the current lot size on NSE, and calculate the notional value per lot.
Divide to get the exact number of lots, then calculate the hedge ratio for rounding down and rounding up.
Choose using the rounding rules, weighing your R-squared, goal, tolerable drawdown and India VIX, and write down your reason.
Set a reminder to recheck the size after any 10% Nifty move, any redemption, and at every roll.

body.label: NSE: Underlyings in the F&O Segment
body.description: Check the current Nifty lot size before every sizing calculation. Lot sizes are revised periodically.

cards.definition: Beta-weighted exposure × target hedge ratio ÷ (Nifty level × lot size).
Lot size × index level. ₹16,25,000 with a lot size of 65 and the Nifty at 25,000.
Buying fewer lots than the exact number. Leaves part of the exposure unprotected.
Buying more lots than the exact number. The excess acts as a bet on a fall, or a buffer against basis risk.
The gradual mismatch between hedge size and exposure caused by market moves, SIPs, redemptions and changing betas.
Roughly one lot of beta-weighted exposure. Below that, any Nifty option hedge is a large over-hedge.

points: Lots needed = beta-weighted exposure × target hedge ratio ÷ (Nifty level × lot size).
The answer is rarely a whole number. Rounding down under-hedges; rounding up adds a bet on a fall.
Round down for index-like portfolios, flexible goals or expensive protection. Round up for basis-heavy portfolios, hard near-term goals or cheap protection, knowingly.
Reducing exposure, or using a closer strike, can get you closer to the exact hedge without fractional lots.
Portfolios below about one lot of beta-weighted exposure cannot be sensibly hedged with Nifty options.
Hedge size drifts with the market, SIPs, redemptions and fund betas. Recalculate at every roll.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Lot sizes, premiums, betas and the basis gap scenario are illustrative. Always use current NSE lot sizes and your own portfolio data. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before hedging your portfolio.
